chunks: "If I swap them, the NMOS goes on top with its drain at V DD and the PMOS goes on the bottom with its drain at ground, gates tied together as before.
The problem is that each device's source is now the output node.
The NMOS turns on only if the gate is a threshold above its source, so when I drive the input high to V DD the output rises until it reaches V DD-V tn , and then the NMOS turns itself off.
With the body effect that's worse, maybe V DD minus 1. 1 volts.
Likewise, the PMOS at the bottom needs its gate a threshold below its source, so when the input goes low the output only gets pulled down to about V tp above ground.
So the output no longer swings rail to rail: it goes between roughly V tp and V DD-V tn . It's also non-inverting: input high gives output high.
And because each device is acting as a source follower, the current drops as the output approaches its limit, so the edges get slower and slower near the end.
There's also a dead zone for mid-range inputs where neither device conducts, so the output just floats.
That's exactly why CMOS is built the other way round: with the PMOS on top, its source is at V DD and the NMOS source is at ground, so each has the full gate drive and the output reaches the rails."
